summary: A review of the Employer stock page found that the tax on your next stock vests ignored the vests earlier in the same year, so a December vest was taxed as if it were the year's first pay. Now the year's earlier vests come first, each tax year's shortfall or refund is shown on its own, and the state's share always shows.
points: Vests already received this year are counted first, so a later vest is taxed at the bracket you have really reached, and the 37% withholding past $1 million of bonus-type pay counts them too.
Each calendar year gets its own sentence: what to set aside by April 15 for that year's return, or what comes back. Withholding in one year cannot pay another year's tax.
The state's share is the state's rate on the vests themselves (Illinois's 4.95% even with no other income), shown whatever the federal figure.
A child is never taken as the person who works there, and pay with no one named, or wages typed on the Federal estimate, count toward the 0.9% Medicare withholding.
Filing separately, selling company shares goes on the return of the person whose account holds them, and this year's sale is stacked on this year's vests.
numbers: $35,900 owed on a December vest after $300,000 of earlier vests (it was shown as $23,364)
$15,000 short when $900,000 vested earlier in the year
$41,850 withheld on a $150,000 vest after $900,000 earlier: 22% on $100,000, 37% on $50,000, 0.9% Medicare

shots.caption: A sample with large vests: after $900,000 that already vested this year, the page says to set aside about $15,000 for the 2026 return and $23,702 for 2027, each on its own line, and about $29,700 of Illinois tax.

summary: A review of the Rental analysis and Home pages found that a couple filing separately got the wrong rental-loss allowance and the wrong home-sale exclusion, and that each rental's tax line could swing wildly when profits and losses nearly cancelled. All fixed, and the property answer key still agrees on every one of its 15,008 rows.
points: Rental: filing separately and living apart, the allowance that lets rental losses come off other income is worked on the income of the return the rentals are on, not both spouses' added up, and the page quotes the separate figures ($12,500, from $50,000 to $75,000).
Rental: each rental's own tax line stays steady when one rental's profit and another's loss nearly cancel; it could swing by thousands of dollars before.
Home: filing separately, a home in neither spouse's name is half each, and each half gets its own $250,000 tax-free.
Home: with no purchase date the page now asks for it instead of quietly assuming two years of ownership, and the tax on a quick sale says how much is the 3.8% investment-income tax.
Both: the 3.8% tax starts at $250,000 for a widow or widower with a child, as the law has it, not $200,000.
numbers: $18,974 of tax for a home in one spouse's name, $0 when it is in neither name (each half under $250,000)
$1,920 and -$1,920: two rentals that cancel, each shown steadily

shots.caption: Two sample rentals whose loss and profit cancel: together they do not change this year's tax, and $8,292 of loss waits for a later year.
A home with a price but no purchase date: the tax-free part is worded 'if you have owned and lived in it two of the last five years', and the page asks for the date.

summary: The tax pages put a sale or a contribution on the return of the spouse who owns the account when a couple files separately, but the Net worth page asked for the owner as a typed name, so no account ever matched a person. Now you choose the owner from the household's people, older typed names are switched over, and each return nets its own sales.
points: Net worth's 'Whose account' is a choice of the people in the household, or 'Joint or shared'. Names typed before that match a person are switched to that person when the plan opens.

Filing separately, the Federal estimate's gains are each return's own: a gain on one spouse's return and a loss on the other's no longer cancel, and the loss carried to next year is worked whenever either return has one.
The Capital gains page takes each spouse's own short-term gain off their own return when it works out the tax those gains add.
A sale named for a third adult in the household is split between the two returns instead of disappearing.
Crypto and Tax lots say the $1,500 yearly loss limit is on each return ($3,000 between you), and Crypto explains when a loss changes nothing because that spouse has no taxable income.
numbers: $3,500 carried to next year from one spouse's $5,000 loss (it showed none)
$1,500 loss limit on each separate return

shots.caption: Net worth's form for a new account: 'Whose account' is now a choice (Joint or shared, or one of the household's people) instead of a typed name.
